 Spain approves a 5.3% minimum wage rise to €1,286 and 4.5% for public servants, 12 days before the election
 Spain’s government approves Tuesday a 5.3% rise in the minimum wage to €1,286 a month and a 4.5% pay rise for public servants for 2027, which Sánchez announced Monday on Telecinco, twelve days before the November 29 election. He says five million workers benefit, and critics say the timing is electoral
 By Platform | 2026-11-17 | 3 min read Share f 𝕏 in t w ✈ L @ The leader of the Spanish government, Pedro Sánchez, announced today that the Council of Ministers will approve, on Tuesday, a 4.5% increase in public servants’ salaries for next year.
 Sánchez made the announcement in an interview with Telecinco, in which he also recalled that, at Tuesday’s meeting, the government will approve the increase in the interprofessional minimum wage (SMI), as Second Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Labor Yolanda Díaz had already stated earlier today.
 The adjustment in the salaries of public servants and employees will be 4.5% for 2027, in accordance with the commitment signed on October 20 between the government and the unions CCOO, UGT, and CSIF, during the meeting of the Monitoring Committee of the Framework Agreement for the Improvement of Public Employment and Citizen Service.
 The head of the executive highlighted, at a time when the election campaign for the November 29 legislative elections is already underway, the policies implemented by his government, contrasting them with a possible setback that, according to Sánchez, would occur if the PP and Vox were to take power.
 Read more about this topic:  Spain’s general strike begins: unions say 41% to 75% turnout in early shifts, employers dispute it, and police detain 27 
 As an example, he cited the increase in the minimum wage over the last eight years, the Efe agency reported.
 The adjustment to this minimum wage, to be approved in the Council of Ministers, will be 5.3%, reaching 1,286 euros gross per month, distributed over fourteen payments (18,004 euros gross per year). In addition, he added that the government will also approve, on Tuesday, the salary increase for public sector workers. According to Sánchez, five million workers will benefit from the executive’s decisions.
 According to the government leader, adding the revaluation of retirement benefits and pensions based on the CPI (Consumer Price Index), around fifteen million citizens will have their purchasing power expanded. Spain has been officially campaigning since Friday for the November 29 legislative elections, with the most recent polls keeping the People’s Party (PP, right-wing) ahead but dependent on Vox (far-right) to form a government.
 Polls agree that the PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, will receive the most votes on November 29, but without an absolute majority, as happened in 2023, when an eight-party coalition ended up enabling a new left-wing executive.
 Read more about this topic:  What caused Sánchez to call for snap elections in Spain? 
 After eight years of governments led by the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and Pedro Sánchez, who in 2023 received 31.68% of the vote and secured 121 deputies, the socialists will once again be the second-largest party this year, but with a vote share below 30% (between 25% and 29.9%) and also with fewer parliamentarians, according to the average of the polls.
 According to the same polls, Vox could surpass 19% of the vote and even double its current bench of 33 deputies in the Spanish parliament.
